opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that today the network effects all accrue to the platform. You use Google, you use Facebook, you use ChatGPT, and every interaction makes their model better and their data moat deeper, but the user doesn't really own any of it. Your context, your history, your preferences are siloed inside each application, and every new app has to start from zero with you.

If you flip that around, and the application actually runs on the user's side, in a confidential environment the user controls, then the user's data and context become the center of gravity. Your personal AI has access to everything about you: your email, your calendar, your health data, your financial information. Because it's running in a secure enclave or a trusted execution environment, the developer of the app can't see it, the cloud provider can't see it, and you can verify that.

That's where the network effect comes in, but it looks different. Instead of one company aggregating everyone's data, you have a layer where developers can build applications that plug into the user's personal AI with the user's permission. Each new app makes every user's AI more capable, and each user's context makes every app more useful from day one. Developers no longer need to collect data to build a good product. They bring the logic, the user brings the context.

Then you add the agent-to-agent piece. If my AI can negotiate with your AI, or coordinate with a merchant's AI, or pool data with other users' AIs in a privacy-preserving way, for example to train a better model or to get a better insurance rate, that's a network effect that belongs to the users rather than to a single intermediary. The more people participate, the more valuable it is for everyone, and the value flows back to the people who generated it.

So for me the bet is that user-owned AI isn't just the ethical choice. It's actually the more powerful architecture, because it removes the friction of every application having to rebuild trust and context from scratch. Once you have that, the composability starts to compound, much like open source did for software.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention embedded monetization or incentives for developers to invest in specialized models.

r002.rationale: It says the user's accumulated context makes each app more useful from day one, giving developers value from building around the user-side AI.

r003.rationale: It says developers no longer need to collect data, but does not identify server-side collection of personal data as a barrier to users adopting apps.

r004.rationale: It describes apps plugging into the user's personal AI, but does not explain that a shared personal data store reduces the need for explicit integrations to expose context.

r005.rationale: It describes apps making the AI more capable and composability compounding, but does not state that apps enrich stored context and thereby attract further app development.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that right now all the network effects in AI accrue to whoever holds the data and the model. You talk to a chatbot, your context, your preferences, your history, all of that lives on their servers, and that's what makes it hard to leave. The lock-in is the moat. So the question we asked ourselves was, what if you flip that, and the application and the data actually run on the user's side, on their device or in a compute environment that they control and that they can move?

The naive view is that this kills network effects, because there's no central aggregator anymore. But I think it actually creates a different kind of network effect, and in some ways a stronger one. If I have a personal AI that holds my context, my data, my keys, and it runs on my side, then every application I use gets better because that AI can carry my context into it. The network effect isn't around the app, it's around the user. The more things my AI can plug into, the more valuable it is to me, and the more valuable it is for a new app to be compatible with it. So developers start building for the user's agent, not for a platform.

And then the second layer is that these agents can talk to each other. If my agent and your agent can negotiate, transact, share verifiable information, that's where a decentralized cloud starts to matter. You need a neutral substrate where identity, payments, and permissions work across all these agents without a single company sitting in the middle taking rent and deciding who's allowed to talk to whom. That's basically what blockchains are good for. Not for running the model, but for coordinating the agents and the value flowing between them.

So the flywheel is: more users with their own agents, more apps built to plug into user-owned agents, more agent-to-agent interactions, and each piece makes the others more valuable. It's a user-centric network effect rather than a platform-centric one. And honestly I think that's the only version of personal AI that makes sense long term, because otherwise you're just rebuilding the same walled gardens with a better interface.

r002.rationale: It says personal AI carries user context into applications, but does not identify accumulated user data as making the user-side cloud more valuable to application developers.

r003.rationale: It describes data held on company servers as a source of lock-in, but does not say server-side personal-data collection deters users from adopting applications.

r004.rationale: It says AI can carry context into applications, but does not explain that a shared personal data store reduces the need for explicit integrations.

r005.rationale: It describes a cycle of more user agents and more compatible applications, but does not say applications enrich stored context and thereby attract further development.

astra-6.text:
I think the network effect comes from moving the center of gravity from individual applications to the user. Today, your information is spread across different services, and each service has a limited view of what you’re trying to do. If applications run on your side, your personal AI can use those capabilities together, with the context you choose to give it.

So a new application doesn’t have to build an entire relationship with you from scratch. It can provide a capability that your AI can discover and use. More useful capabilities make the personal AI more valuable, more users attract developers, and developers bring more capabilities.

Then there’s another layer, where personal AIs can interact. If I want to organize something with you, our assistants could coordinate without either of us having to manually move information between applications. The important part is that this happens under our control. That’s where I see the potential for a network: applications and agents working together on behalf of users.

r003.rationale: It does not describe developers collecting personal data on their servers as a barrier to adoption.

r004.rationale: It discusses shared context and coordination, but does not explain that storing application context in a shared personal data store removes the need for explicit integrations.

r005.rationale: It describes more useful capabilities attracting users and users attracting developers, but not applications enriching stored context and thereby attracting further application development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the network effect comes from your personal AI being able to interact with other people’s AIs and with applications on your behalf. It has your context, it understands what you’re trying to do, and you control what information it shares.

For example, if we want to organize something together, our assistants should be able to coordinate without everybody having to join the same application and manually enter all their information again. As more people and services become accessible this way, your assistant becomes more useful. And developers get access to users through those assistants without having to build the entire relationship from scratch.

The important part is that the context stays with the user. You can try a new application, give it permission to do a particular task, and bring your existing context with you. So the network effect starts to form around the user and the connections between users, rather than around one application that holds everybody’s data.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention embedded monetization or specialized models.

r002.rationale: It says developers can reach users through assistants, but does not identify accumulated user data as a reason the user-side cloud becomes more valuable to application developers.

r003.rationale: It mentions avoiding repeated manual data entry, but not developers collecting personal data on their servers as a barrier to adoption.

r004.rationale: It says users can bring existing context to new applications, but does not explain that storing application context in a shared personal data store reduces the need for explicit integrations.

r005.rationale: It describes assistants becoming more useful as more people and services become accessible, but not a cycle in which applications enrich stored user context and thereby attract further application development.
